newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-Cultus sees large NZ oilfield.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Cultus sees large NZ oilfield.

text.p: Cultus Petroleum NL's Maari oilfield offshore New Zealand could produce about 100 million barrels of black gold after drilling starts later this year, managing director Don Beard said on Thursday.
In a telephone interview with Reuters from Sydney, Beard said the Maari field, offshore Taranaki in block PEP38413, could become one of New Zealand's largest oilfields.
"We see the potential for around about 100 million barrels of oil," Beard said, adding there was no doubt that there was oil there.
"There's been a couple of wells drilled there before, one in 1973 and one in 1984, and they produced oil in those days at about 1,000 barrels a day," Beard said.
"We've since found that those formations were damaged and they would produce at a better rate than that, plus we think we're smart enough to drill in a better spot.
"So putting that all together, we think there's potential for quite a big field there."

Ministery of Commerce statistics show that the largest oilfield in New Zealand at present is McKee, onshore Taranaki, which has 10.2 million barrels left in reserve. When discovered in 1980, it had reserves of 53.14 million barrels.
Beard said the Maari field, which consisted of two features, could be expected to produce somewhere between 20,000 and 40,000 barrels of oil a day.
"It really depends on the testing process, but you might expect a 100 million barrel field to be making in excess of somewhere in between 20,000 and 40,000 barrels a day," he said.
"100 million barrels is a large field."
On Thursday, crude oil was priced at about US$19.50 (NZ$28.34) a barrel.
Beard said Cultus was in the process of "farming out" about 70 percent of the investment to a well-known, major international company, which he declined to name.

"We have 100 percent of that area. We're in the throes of farming that out, in other words letting another company come in, and they will pay our way through a well or two, and for that we'll give them some interest," he said.

"That's happening right now. We're actually dotting the Is and crossing the Ts with a major company. It's an international company and it will come in and then lead the venture basically, but we'll still be sitting there with about 30 percent of the investment."
He said he expected the agreement to be sewn up within a month. Drilling was expected to start in November or December this year, depending on the availability of rigs.
Beard said Cultus, just under 30 percent owned by New Zealand merchant bankers Fay Richwhite, had other interests in New Zealand and considered the country a good prospect.
"We like New Zealand, we like the prospectivity there. We think there's quite a bit of potential there, particularly in the offshore (area)," he said.
In addition to the offshore block, Cultus also had a small interest in a couple of onshore blocks in the Taranaki.

"Plus we just picked up a 20 or 25 percent share in two blocks in the Westland Basin in the South Island. That's all very preliminary sort of exploration there. We're in there with New Zealand Oil and Gas," Beard said.
He said finding good oil and gas fields was like detective work. "You just keep following the leads up and what was yesterday's garbage becomes tomorrow's treasures."
The majority of Cultus's operations are in Australia, where the company has several oil and gas fields.
Cultus is listed in both Australia and New Zealand.

Since January 1996, its share price has risen 640 percent in New Zealand and 738 percent in Australia to NZ$3.20 and A$2.88 on Thursday, primarily on oil and gas discoveries and the prospects of others.
Beard said he did not believe the current share price was over-rated and was optimistic it would rise more in due course.
"It's a fairly complex business and it is a business that takes enormous risks, but people seem to like it," he said.
--Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 4734746
